pos: n. (an inordinate desire of gain; greediness after wealth)
etymology: Latin avaritia, from avere, to crave. The older English distinguishes avarice, the craving to get, from covetousness, the craving for what is another's; Scripture treats them as one disease.
biblical_def: Avarice is the inordinate desire of gain, and the Lord warns against it in a way that anticipates every defence: “Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth” (Luk 12:15). Paul names it a root: “the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows” (1Ti 6:10). He classes it with idolatry: “covetousness, which is idolatry” (Col 3:5). Proverbs names the end: “so are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof” (Pro 1:19). And the Preacher names the mechanism: “He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver” (Ecc 5:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines avarice as an inordinate desire of gaining and possessing wealth; covetousness; greediness or insatiable desire of gain.
webster_full: AVARICE, n. An inordinate desire of gaining and possessing wealth; covetousness; greediness or insatiable desire of gain.
Avarice is the vice of declining years.
2. An inordinate desire of other things; as an avarice of praise.
AVARICIOUS, a. Covetous; greedy of gain; immoderately desirous of accumulating property.
scriptures: And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
Col 3:5
Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry:
Pro 1:19
So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof.
Ecc 5:10
He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity.
corruption_summary: Avarice is the one sin nobody confesses, because it is always the next man who has too much.
corruption_paragraphs: Every other sin has a threshold a man can admit he has crossed. Avarice does not, because the standard is always set just above one's own holdings; the greedy man is the one with more, and the man with less is prudent rather than poor. This is why the Lord prefaces His warning with take heed, and beware — a doubled caution He does not attach to adultery or theft. The sin hides inside ordinary financial competence, and a congregation will discipline a drunkard for years before it notices a covetous elder.

Colossians 3:5 supplies the diagnosis that explains the persistence: covetousness which is idolatry. It is not merely that money can be loved too much; it is that money offers what God offers — security, standing, freedom, a future — and does so without requiring faith. That is why 1 Timothy 6:10 says those who coveted after it have erred from the faith, since a man who has secured his soul elsewhere no longer needs the promises. The piercing with many sorrows comes afterwards, when the security proves to be exactly as durable as a currency.

Ecclesiastes 5:10 states the trap in the plainest form available: he that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver. The appetite is structurally incapable of being met by its object, so more of the object cannot cure it. Every generation rediscovers this and none acts on it. The remedy Scripture gives is not a lower income but a different set of affections — contentment, which Paul says he learned (Php 4:11), and generosity, which is avarice run in reverse and is the only spending that reliably weakens the love of money.
roots_summary: Greek pleonexia (G4124), covetousness, a desire for more; philarguria (G5365), love of money; Hebrew betsa (H1215), unjust gain; ahab keseph (H157, H3701), to love silver.
roots_lines: Greek pleonexia (G4124) — literally the desire for more; Luke 12:15, Colossians 3:5, Ephesians 5:3, Mark 7:22.
Greek philarguria (G5365) — love of money; 1 Timothy 6:10 only; the adjective philarguros, Luke 16:14, 2 Timothy 3:2.
Hebrew betsa (H1215) — gain, unjust profit; Proverbs 1:19, 28:16, Exodus 18:21, Jeremiah 6:13.
usage: “Take heed, and beware” — a doubled caution, attached to this sin.
“Covetousness, which is idolatry” — because it offers what God offers.
“He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver” — more cannot cure it.

pos: n. (eager or inordinate desire; the appetite in its unlawful reach)
etymology: Latin cupiditas, from cupere, to desire — the root of Cupid, who is desire personified. Augustine's cupiditas is love aimed at the wrong object, and stands against caritas.
biblical_def: Cupidity is desire out of bounds. The Tenth Commandment forbids it as an inward act: “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife” (Exo 20:17), and Paul says this was the commandment that exposed him: “I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet” (Rom 7:7). James traces the sequence: “every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin” (Jas 1:14–15), and finds it behind conflict: “ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have” (Jas 4:2). John maps the whole field: “the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1Jn 2:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cupidity as an eager desire to possess something; an ardent wishing or longing; inordinate or unlawful desire of wealth or objects of sense.
webster_full: CUPIDITY, n. An eager desire to possess something; an ardent wishing or longing; inordinate or unlawful desire of wealth or objects of sense.
Cupidity is not used, I believe, for the animal appetite for food, but for wealth, honor, and things of an intellectual or moral nature.
scriptures: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's.
Rom 7:7
What shall we say then? Is the law sin? God forbid. Nay, I had not known sin, but by the law: for I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet.
Jas 1:14
But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.
Jas 4:2
Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain: ye fight and war, yet ye have not, because ye ask not.
For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.
corruption_summary: Desire itself is treated as the sin, or as innocent whatever its object, and the Bible does neither.
corruption_paragraphs: One error makes wanting sinful. That is asceticism rather than Christianity: God made hunger, thirst, delight in beauty and the desire of a man for a wife, called the creation very good, and promises a feast at the end of the story. Psalm 37:4 tells the believer to delight himself in the LORD and says He shall give thee the desires of thine heart. Desire is a created faculty and its disorder is a corruption of something good, which is the Reformed account of every sin.

The opposite error, far commoner now, treats desire as self-justifying — the wanting proves the thing is right for me, and the only sin would be denying it. The Tenth Commandment stands directly against that, and it is the commandment that makes the Decalogue impossible to keep externally. The other nine can be satisfied by a man who never acts; this one reaches into what he wishes he could do, which is why Paul says it was this commandment that killed him. A moralist may keep his hands clean for a lifetime and be undone by the tenth word.

James 1:14–15 is the anatomy, and its value is the sequence: drawn away of his own lust — the bait is internal, not merely circumstantial — then enticed, then conception, then sin, then death when it is finished. Every stage is reversible until the last, and the point of naming them is that a man can intervene early. Waiting until the act is in view is waiting until the hardest possible moment. Augustine's contrast is the practical remedy: cupiditas is not defeated by suppression but displaced by caritas, a stronger love aimed at a better object.
roots_summary: Greek epithumia (G1939), desire, lust; hedone (G2237), pleasure; Hebrew chamad (H2530), to covet, desire; avah (H183), to long after.
roots_lines: Hebrew chamad (H2530) — to covet, desire; Exodus 20:17, Joshua 7:21, Micah 2:2.
Greek epithumia (G1939) — desire, lust; Romans 7:7–8, James 1:14–15, 1 John 2:16–17 — also used of good desire, Luke 22:15.
Greek hedone (G2237) — pleasure; James 4:1–3, Titus 3:3, 2 Peter 2:13.
usage: “I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet”.
“Drawn away of his own lust” — the bait is internal.
“Ye lust, and have not” — James, explaining where church fights come from.

pos: n. (excessive liberty; the abuse of freedom into contempt for law)
etymology: Latin licentia, leave or permission — the same root as licence. The word describes what happens when permission is taken as unlimited: liberty turned loose from law.
biblical_def: Licentiousness is liberty turned into licence. Jude names the men who do it: “ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness, and denying the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ” (Jud 1:4). Paul forbids the move in the same breath as he grants the freedom: “ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another” (Gal 5:13). Peter exposes the promise as false: “while they promise them liberty, they themselves are the servants of corruption” (2Pe 2:19), and adds, “as free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness” (1Pe 2:16). Paul's own answer to the charge is a recoil: “Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid” (Rom 6:1–2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines licentiousness as excessive indulgence of liberty; contempt of the just restraints of law, morality and decorum.
webster_full: LICENTIOUSNESS, n. Excessive indulgence of liberty; contempt of the just restraints of law, morality and decorum.
The licentiousness of authors is not to be tolerated.
2. Dissoluteness; debauchery; lewdness.
LICENTIOUS, a. Using license; indulging freedom to excess; unrestrained by law or morality; loose; dissolute.
scriptures: Jud 1:4

For there are certain men crept in unawares, who were before of old ordained to this condemnation, ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness, and denying the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ.
Gal 5:13
For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another.
While they promise them liberty, they themselves are the servants of corruption: for of whom a man is overcome, of the same is he brought in bondage.
As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God.
Rom 6:1
What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?
corruption_summary: Grace is preached as though it removed the law's authority as well as its condemnation, and Paul saw the inference coming.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 6:1 is proof that Paul preached grace properly, because it is the objection his doctrine invites. A gospel nobody could possibly mistake for a licence to sin has not said enough about grace; a gospel that answers the objection with God forbid and then six chapters of argument has. His reply is not a retreat into conditions but a fact about what happened: how shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein? The believer's problem with continuing in sin is not that it is forbidden but that it is now unnatural.

Second Peter 2:19 exposes the marketing. They promise liberty and are themselves the servants of corruption — the offer is made by men who are demonstrably not free, and everyone can see it except the ones buying. This is the reliable test of every licentious teaching: look at the teacher's own bondage. Licence never delivers freedom, because a man ruled by his appetites is ruled, and calling the ruler himself changes nothing about the arrangement.

Galatians 5:13 gives the positive form and it is startling in its economy: called unto liberty, and then by love serve one another — the word is the verb for slave-service. Christian freedom is not freedom from all masters but freedom from a master who destroys, in order to bind oneself voluntarily to the good of one's neighbour. That is why the same chapter can list the works of the flesh and the fruit of the Spirit without any tension: the free man is not the one with no obligations but the one whose obligations he has come to love.
roots_summary: Greek aselgeia (G766), lasciviousness, wantonness; eleutheria (G1657), liberty; aphorme (G874), occasion, base of operations; epikalumma (G1942), a cloke, cover.
roots_lines: Greek aselgeia (G766) — lasciviousness, unrestrained conduct; Jude 1:4, Galatians 5:19, 2 Peter 2:2, 2:18.
Greek aphorme (G874) — occasion, a base from which to operate; Galatians 5:13, Romans 7:8, 7:11.
Greek epikalumma (G1942) — a cloke, covering; 1 Peter 2:16 only.
usage: “Turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness” — the grace itself is the material.
“They promise them liberty” — and are themselves the servants of corruption.
“By love serve one another” — and the verb is slave-service.

pos: n. (free indulgence in costly food, dress or equipage; voluptuousness)
etymology: Latin luxuria, rankness, excess — originally of plants growing beyond their proper form. The older English sense is nearer lewdness; the modern one is expenditure beyond need.
biblical_def: Luxury is indulgence beyond need. The rich man of the parable “was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day” while Lazarus lay at his gate (Luk 16:19). Amos indicts a nation for it: “That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches… but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph” (Amo 6:4–6). James makes it a charge at the judgment: “Ye have lived in pleasure on the earth, and been wanton; ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter” (Jas 5:5). Paul says of the self-indulgent widow, “she that liveth in pleasure is dead while she liveth” (1Ti 5:6). And the Lord notes where soft clothing belongs: “they which are gorgeously apparelled, and live delicately, are in kings' courts” (Luk 7:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines luxury as a free or extravagant indulgence in the pleasures of the table, in dress and equipage; voluptuousness; and anything delightful to the senses.
webster_full: LUXURY, n. A free or extravagant indulgence in the pleasures of the table, as in rich and expensive diet, or delicious food and liquors; voluptuousness in the gratification of appetite.
2. A free or extravagant indulgence in dress, equipage and furniture.
3. Any thing delightful to the senses.
4. Lust; lewd desire.
scriptures: There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day:
Amo 6:4
That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall;
Jas 5:5
Ye have lived in pleasure on the earth, and been wanton; ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter.
But she that liveth in pleasure is dead while she liveth.
Luk 7:25
But what went ye out for to see? A man clothed in soft raiment? Behold, they which are gorgeously apparelled, and live delicately, are in kings' courts.
corruption_summary: The sin is located in the goods rather than in the indifference, and Amos convicts the couches by what the men on them failed to notice.
corruption_paragraphs: Amos 6 is the most precise passage on this and its logic is easily missed. The prophet catalogues the ivory beds, the lambs out of the flock, the wine drunk in bowls and the chief ointments — and the indictment arrives in the last clause: but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph. The luxury is condemned by what it made them incapable of feeling. The nation was coming apart and the men who could have acted had insulated themselves so thoroughly that they had not noticed. That is the mechanism, and it works identically at any income.

The parable makes the same point by omission. The rich man is never accused of fraud, cruelty or oppression; nothing suggests he sent Lazarus away. He is condemned for a beggar at his own gate whom he had simply stopped seeing, and the details of the purple and the daily feasting are there to explain how a man arrives at that. Luxury does its damage less by what it consumes than by the distance it builds, and a life arranged so that need is never encountered will reliably produce a heart that cannot be moved by it.

This is not an argument for asceticism, and Scripture refuses to supply one. God gives richly all things to enjoy, the Lord made wine at a wedding, and Ecclesiastes commends eating one's bread with joy. The question is never the sum spent but two others: whether the spending has made a man deaf, and whether he could stop. First Timothy 5:6 is the sharpest verdict — she that liveth in pleasure is dead while she liveth — because a life organised entirely around its own comfort is describable as a death that has not yet been noticed.
roots_summary: Greek truphao (G5171), to live delicately, riot; spatalao (G4684), to live in pleasure, be wanton; lampros (G2988), splendid, gorgeous; Hebrew sarach (H5628), to stretch oneself out.
roots_lines: Greek truphe / truphao (G5172, G5171) — delicate living, riot; Luke 7:25, James 5:5, 2 Peter 2:13.
Greek spatalao (G4684) — to live in pleasure, be wanton; 1 Timothy 5:6, James 5:5 — both occurrences.
Greek euphraino lampros (G2165, G2988) — fared sumptuously; Luke 16:19.
usage: “But they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph” — the indictment, in the last clause.
“Fared sumptuously every day” — and a beggar at his own gate.
“Dead while she liveth” — a death not yet noticed.

pos: n. (contemptuous pride in speech or bearing; overbearing contempt of others)
etymology: Latin insolens, unaccustomed, immoderate — from in-, not, and solere, to be wont. The insolent man behaves in a way that is not customary, having exempted himself from the ordinary courtesies.
biblical_def: Insolence is pride made audible. Proverbs gives it a name: “Proud and haughty scorner is his name, who dealeth in proud wrath” (Pro 21:24). Paul lists it among the marks of the last days — men shall be “boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy” (2Ti 3:2) — and among the fruits of a reprobate mind, “despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things” (Rom 1:30). The psalmist prays under it: “our soul is exceedingly filled with the scorning of those that are at ease, and with the contempt of the proud” (Psa 123:4). And Daniel records what it costs a king: “when his heart was lifted up, and his mind hardened in pride, he was deposed from his kingly throne” (Dan 5:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines insolence as pride or haughtiness manifested in contemptuous and overbearing treatment of others; and insolent as proud and haughty, with contempt of others.
webster_full: INSOLENCE, n. Pride or haughtiness manifested in contemptuous and overbearing treatment of others; petulant contempt; impudence.
Flown with insolence and wine.
INSOLENT, a. Proud and haughty, with contempt of others; overbearing; domineering in power.
2. Proceeding from insolence; insulting; as insolent words or behavior.
scriptures: Proud and haughty scorner is his name, who dealeth in proud wrath.
For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,
Rom 1:30
Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents,
Our soul is exceedingly filled with the scorning of those that are at ease, and with the contempt of the proud.
Dan 5:20
But when his heart was lifted up, and his mind hardened in pride, he was deposed from his kingly throne, and they took his glory from him:
corruption_summary: Insolence is excused as candour, and the man who wounds by habit says he is only being direct.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest disguise is honesty. A man who speaks contemptuously to those beneath him, cuts off anyone who differs, and treats a question as an affront will describe himself as plain-spoken and impatient with nonsense — and there is always a genuine virtue nearby that the vice can borrow clothes from. The test Proverbs supplies is proud wrath: not whether the words were true, but what they were carrying. Truth is not less true when spoken kindly, so a habitual choice of the wounding form has to be explained by something other than a love of accuracy.

Daniel 5:20 traces the arc that makes insolence a spiritual and not merely a social problem. Nebuchadnezzar's heart was lifted up, his mind hardened in pride, and he was deposed — and Daniel is recounting this to Belshazzar, who knew all of it and did the same thing anyway. That is the note the chapter ends on: thou hast not humbled thine heart, though thou knewest all this. Insolence is not chiefly a failure of manners; it is a posture toward God that shows itself first toward men, and information does not cure it.

Psalm 123 is worth setting alongside, because it is written from underneath. The scorning of those that are at ease and the contempt of the proud is a real affliction and the psalm does not tell the sufferer to shrug it off; it lifts his eyes to God as the eyes of servants look unto the hand of their masters, and asks for mercy. Insolence damages people, and the Bible treats being on the receiving end of it as a grief to be brought to God rather than a slight to be absorbed silently.
roots_summary: Greek hubristes (G5197), an insolent man, despiteful; huperephanos (G5244), proud, showing oneself above; Hebrew zed (H2086), proud, arrogant; luts (H3887), to scorn.
roots_lines: Greek hubristes (G5197) — insolent, despiteful; Romans 1:30, 1 Timothy 1:13.
Greek huperephanos (G5244) — proud; 2 Timothy 3:2, James 4:6, 1 Peter 5:5, Luke 1:51.
Hebrew lets (H3887) — scorner; Proverbs 21:24, 9:7–8, 13:1, 22:10.
usage: “Proud and haughty scorner is his name” — Proverbs gives him a name.
“Though thou knewest all this” — and information did not cure it.
“The contempt of the proud” — a grief to bring to God.

pos: n. (shamelessness; impudence in doing or saying what should cause a blush)
etymology: French effronterie, from Latin ex-, out, and frons, the forehead — the brow that cannot be made to redden. Scripture's own figure is identical: a forehead of brass, a face that will not blush.
biblical_def: Effrontery is the loss of the capacity for shame. Jeremiah names it as a stage in a nation's decline: “Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush” (Jer 6:15, repeated at Jer 8:12). Ezekiel is sent to “impudent children and stiffhearted” (Eze 2:4). Proverbs shows it in the strange woman, who “caught him, and kissed him, and with an impudent face said unto him” (Pro 7:13). Paul describes men “whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things” (Php 3:19). And Isaiah records Sodom's last stage: “they declare their sin as Sodom, they hide it not” (Isa 3:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines effrontery as impudence; audaciousness; shamelessness; assurance; a modest man may show a becoming boldness, but an impudent man only can be guilty of effrontery.
webster_full: EFFRONTERY, n. Impudence; audaciousness; shamelessness; boldness; sauciness.
It is impudence and effrontery that supply the place of merit.
Effrontery is a sure mark of ill-breeding, and often of guilt.
scriptures: Jer 6:15

Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush: therefore they shall fall among them that fall: at the time that I visit them they shall be cast down, saith the LORD.
Eze 2:4
For they are impudent children and stiffhearted. I do send thee unto them; and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD.
Pro 7:13
So she caught him, and kissed him, and with an impudent face said unto him,
Php 3:19
Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.)
Isa 3:9
The shew of their countenance doth witness against them; and they declare their sin as Sodom, they hide it not. Woe unto their soul! for they have rewarded evil unto themselves.
corruption_summary: Shamelessness is mistaken for courage, and the inability to blush is a symptom rather than a strength.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 6:15 describes a specific and late stage of moral decline and its wording is careful: they were not ashamed, neither could they blush. Not would not — could not. The faculty had gone. Shame in Scripture is not the same as guilt: guilt is the objective state and shame is the God-given signal that registers it, and a conscience seared over time stops producing the signal while the state remains. That is why the loss is worse than the sin that caused it. A man who feels nothing has lost the alarm, not the fire.

The modern confusion runs the other way and it is worth naming, because shame has become a word almost entirely negative in usage. There is a false shame that Scripture works to destroy — the shame the forgiven feel over sins that are covered, the shame imposed by other people's judgments, the shame of the gospel that Paul refuses (I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ). Destroying that is a mercy. But a Christianity that treats every experience of shame as an injury to be healed has no vocabulary left for Jeremiah's diagnosis, and will read the inability to blush as freedom.

Philippians 3:19 gives the terminal form: whose glory is in their shame. Not indifference to shame but pride in it — the thing that once would have been hidden is now the boast, and the sequence in Isaiah 3:9 is the same, since the last step before judgment is that they declare their sin and hide it not. The remedy in every case is the same one Ezekiel was sent with, which is the word of God delivered to hard foreheads by a prophet God warned in advance that they would not listen — and told to speak anyway.
roots_summary: Hebrew kalam (H3637), to be ashamed, confounded; bosh (H954), to blush, be ashamed; az panim (H5810, H6440), hard of face, impudent; Greek aischune (G152), shame.
roots_lines: Hebrew bosh (H954) — to be ashamed, to blush; Jeremiah 6:15, 8:12, Ezra 9:6.
Hebrew chazqe metsach (H2389, H4696) — hard of forehead, impudent; Ezekiel 2:4, 3:7–9.
Greek aischune (G152) — shame; Philippians 3:19, Hebrews 12:2, Jude 1:13.
usage: “Neither could they blush” — could not, and that is the diagnosis.
“Whose glory is in their shame” — the terminal form.
“They declare their sin as Sodom, they hide it not”.

pos: n. (peevishness; a fretful irritability that takes offence at trifles)
etymology: Latin petulantia, from petere, to seek or attack — the petulant man is always slightly on the attack. Calvin uses the word constantly of his opponents' tone rather than their arguments.
biblical_def: Petulance is anger on a hair-trigger over small things. Proverbs marks it as folly: “He that is soon angry dealeth foolishly” (Pro 14:17), and its opposite as glory: “The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression” (Pro 19:11). James makes the connection explicit: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: for the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” (Jas 1:19–20). Paul commands its removal: “let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you” (Eph 4:31). And Jonah supplies the definitive case, angry over a gourd, asked twice, “Doest thou well to be angry?” (Jon 4:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines petulance as freakish passion; peevishness; pettishness; sauciness; and petulant as apt to be pettish or fretful without cause.
webster_full: PETULANCE, PETULANCY, n. Freakish passion; peevishness; pettishness; sauciness; as the petulance of youth.
PETULANT, a. Saucy; pert; froward; forward; insolent.
2. Manifesting petulance; proceeding from pettishness; capricious.
PETULANTLY, adv. With saucy pertness.
scriptures: He that is soon angry dealeth foolishly: and a man of wicked devices is hated.
The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression.
Jas 1:19
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
Eph 4:31
Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice:
Jon 4:9
And God said to Jonah, Doest thou well to be angry for the gourd? And he said, I do well to be angry, even unto death.
corruption_summary: Peevishness is treated as a temperament rather than a sin, and the small size of the provocation is taken as an excuse rather than as the evidence.
corruption_paragraphs: The book of Jonah spends three chapters on a great fish, a great city and a great repentance, and then gives its whole fourth chapter to a prophet sulking over a plant. That is deliberate. God asks him twice whether he does well to be angry, and Jonah's answer — I do well to be angry, even unto death — is the most self-aware sentence a petulant man ever spoke, because he means it. The book ends on God's question about the hundred and twenty thousand persons in Nineveh who could not discern their right hand from their left, and it ends without Jonah's reply. The reader is left to supply his own.

The excuse in every congregation is temperament: he has always been touchy, that is just how she is. But Ephesians 4:31 lists wrath and clamour among things to be put away, which is a command addressed to people who can obey it, and puts the remedy in the following verse — be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you. The argument is not that the offence was small but that the forgiveness received was large, which reframes the whole calculation.

Proverbs 19:11 is the verse to memorise, and its most striking word is glory. It is a man's glory to pass over a transgression — not his loss, not his weakness, not a concession he makes at cost to his dignity. The world reads a refusal to take offence as a failure of self-respect. Scripture reads it as the height of a man's dignity, and the reason is in the pattern: God passes over transgressions at infinite cost, and the man who can do it in miniature is doing the most godlike thing available to him that day.
roots_summary: Greek orge (G3709), settled wrath; thumos (G2372), hot anger, rage; kraugé (G2906), clamour; Hebrew qatsar aph (H7116, H639), short of nostril, soon angry.
roots_lines: Hebrew qetsar appayim (H7116 with H639) — short-tempered, soon angry; Proverbs 14:17, 14:29.
Greek thumos (G2372) — hot anger, rage; Ephesians 4:31, Galatians 5:20, Colossians 3:8.
Greek bradus eis orgen (G1021, G3709) — slow to wrath; James 1:19–20.
usage: “Doest thou well to be angry for the gourd?” — asked twice, and answered badly.
“The wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” — however righteous it feels.
“It is his glory to pass over a transgression” — his glory, not his loss.

pos: v. (to claim or assume unduly; to take to oneself what belongs to another, especially to God)
etymology: Latin arrogare, to claim for oneself, from ad-, to, and rogare, to ask. Calvin's constant charge against both Rome and the free-will party is that man arrogates to himself what belongs to God alone.
biblical_def: To arrogate is to claim what is not one's own, and the archetype is a claim on God's glory. He states the boundary: “I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another” (Isa 42:8). Nebuchadnezzar crosses it: “Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?” (Dan 4:30). Herod accepts the shout “It is the voice of a god, and not of a man”, and “gave not God the glory” (Act 12:22–23). Lucifer's five “I wills” end in “I will be like the most High” (Isa 14:13–14). And the man of sin “exalteth himself above all that is called God” (2Th 2:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines arrogate as to assume, demand or challenge more than is proper; to make undue claims, from vanity or false pretensions to right or merit.
webster_full: ARROGATE, v.t. To assume, demand or challenge more than is proper; to make undue claims, from vanity or false pretensions to right or merit.
ARROGATION, n. The act of arrogating, or making exorbitant claims; the act of taking more than one is justly entitled to.
ARROGANT, a. Assuming; making or having the disposition to make exorbitant claims of rank or estimation.
scriptures: Isa 42:8
I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images.
Dan 4:30
The king spake, and said, Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?
And the people gave a shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man.
For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north:
Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; so that he as God sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself that he is God.
corruption_summary: The dramatic cases are studied and the ordinary one is missed, which is a man taking credit for grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Herod, Nebuchadnezzar and Lucifer make the doctrine easy to admire and easy to avoid, because no one in the pews is accepting divine honours. The Reformation quarrel located the same sin somewhere far less theatrical: in a doctrine of salvation where the decisive contribution is man's. If grace makes salvation possible and the will makes it actual, then the difference between the saved and the lost is finally in the man, and he has something to glory in that he did not receive — which is precisely what 1 Corinthians 4:7 forbids. That is arrogation in a Sunday coat.

Isaiah 42:8 gives the reason God will not share, and it is not divine touchiness. He is the only being for whom self-regard is not a vice, because He is in fact the highest good, and to direct worship elsewhere is to lie about reality and to injure the worshipper. Every idol is a smaller thing given a weight it cannot bear, and it breaks under it. When God refuses to give His glory to another He is refusing to endorse a falsehood that would ruin us.

Acts 12 records the sentence with a detail Luke wanted kept: the people cried that it was the voice of a god, and immediately the angel of the Lord smote him because he gave not God the glory. The sin was not the shout, which he did not organise, but the silence — he received what was offered and said nothing. Compare Paul and Barnabas at Lystra, who tore their clothes and ran in among the people crying we also are men of like passions with you. The two scenes are placed in the same book, a few chapters apart, and between them lies the whole of what it means not to arrogate.
roots_summary: Hebrew kabod (H3519), glory, weight; alah (H5927), to ascend; Greek doxa (G1391), glory; huperairomai (G5229), to exalt oneself above.
roots_lines: Hebrew kabod (H3519) — glory, weight, honour; Isaiah 42:8, 48:11, Exodus 33:18.
Greek huperairomai (G5229) — to exalt oneself exceedingly; 2 Thessalonians 2:4, 2 Corinthians 12:7.
Greek ouk edoken ten doxan to theo (G1391) — gave not God the glory; Acts 12:23.
usage: “My glory will I not give to another” — and the refusal is a mercy.
“Because he gave not God the glory” — the sin was the silence.
“We also are men of like passions with you” — the other response, in the same book.

pos: adj. (hateful; enormously wicked; of a crime aggravated beyond the common sort)
etymology: Old French haineus, hateful, from hair, to hate. The AV uses it once, of adultery: “this is an heinous crime” (Job 31:11).
biblical_def: A heinous sin is one aggravated beyond the ordinary. Job uses the word of adultery: “For this is an heinous crime; yea, it is an iniquity to be punished by the judges” (Job 31:11). Ezekiel is shown Israel's abominations in ascending order, told each time to “turn thee yet again, and thou shalt see greater abominations” (Eze 8:6). Jeremiah names a national version: “A wonderful and horrible thing is committed in the land” (Jer 5:30). God says of Sodom, “their sin is very grievous” (Gen 18:20). And Nathan tells David that his aggravation was the dishonour done to God's name: “thou hast given great occasion to the enemies of the LORD to blaspheme” (2Sa 12:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines heinous as hateful; hence, great, enormous, aggravated; as a heinous crime; and heinousness as enormity, atrociousness.
webster_full: HEINOUS, a. Properly, hateful; hence, great, enormous, aggravated; as a heinous crime.
HEINOUSLY, adv. Hatefully; abominably; enormously.
HEINOUSNESS, n. Odiousness; enormity; atrociousness; as the heinousness of a crime.
scriptures: For this is an heinous crime; yea, it is an iniquity to be punished by the judges.
Eze 8:6

He said furthermore unto me, Son of man, seest thou what they do? even the great abominations that the house of Israel committeth here, that I should go far off from my sanctuary? but turn thee yet again, and thou shalt see greater abominations.
Jer 5:30
A wonderful and horrible thing is committed in the land;
And the LORD said, Because the cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and because their sin is very grievous;
Howbeit, because by this deed thou hast given great occasion to the enemies of the LORD to blaspheme, the child also that is born unto thee shall surely die.
corruption_summary: All sins are said to be equal before God, and Scripture grades them constantly.
corruption_paragraphs: The pulpit formula that all sins are equal is trying to say something true and says it wrongly. What is true is that any sin is enough to condemn, and that no man's comparative record gives him standing before God. What is false is that Scripture treats them alike. Ezekiel is walked through a temple and shown greater abominations by degree; the Lord tells Pilate that he who delivered Him up has the greater sin; Sodom's sin is very grievous; He speaks of the weightier matters of the law. A doctrine that makes a harsh word and a murder identical has to ignore all of it, and it does real damage in counselling rooms.

The Reformed catechisms handle this properly by listing what aggravates a sin: the person offended, the person offending, the light he sinned against, the office he held, the relation he stood in, the deliberation, and the scandal caused. Second Samuel 12:14 is the classic instance — David's sin is aggravated not because adultery is the worst of crimes but because of who he was and what his fall gave the enemies of the LORD occasion to say. The same act, by a different man, in a different office, is not the same act in the reckoning of heaven.

The pastoral use runs both ways and both are needed. To the man crushed by a grave sin: it is as heinous as he fears and there is a Saviour proportioned to it, since the blood of Christ was not calculated against a sliding scale. To the respectable person who has never done anything scandalous: the absence of heinous sins is not innocence, and the catechism's list of aggravations includes sinning against light, which is exactly the situation of a lifelong churchgoer. Neither party is served by the flattening formula.
roots_summary: Hebrew zimmah (H2154), a wicked purpose, heinous crime; toebah (H8441), abomination; shaarurah (H8186), a horrible thing; rabbah meod (H7227), very grievous.
roots_lines: Hebrew zimmah (H2154) — lewdness, a heinous crime; Job 31:11, Leviticus 18:17, Ezekiel 16:27.
Hebrew toebah (H8441) — abomination; Ezekiel 8:6–17, Proverbs 6:16, Deuteronomy 18:12.
Hebrew shaarurah (H8186) — a horrible thing; Jeremiah 5:30, 18:13, 23:14, Hosea 6:10.
usage: “This is an heinous crime” — the AV's one use, and it is Job's.
“Thou shalt see greater abominations” — graded, three times over.
“Great occasion to the enemies of the LORD to blaspheme” — what aggravated David's.

pos: n. (public disgrace; dishonour attached to a name)
etymology: Latin ignominia, from in-, not, and nomen, name — the loss of one's name, of the good report by which a man is known. The AV uses it once (Pro 18:3).
biblical_def: Ignominy is public disgrace. Proverbs pairs it with contempt: “When the wicked cometh, then cometh also contempt, and with ignominy reproach” (Pro 18:3). It is what the Servant bore: “He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him” (Isa 53:3). Christ took it deliberately, “who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God” (Heb 12:2), dying “even the death of the cross” (Php 2:8). And His people are called out to where it is: “let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb 13:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ignominy as public disgrace; shame; reproach; dishonor; infamy; and, in a general sense, the loss of character or reputation.
webster_full: IGNOMINY, n. Public disgrace; shame; reproach; dishonor; infamy.
Their generals have been received with honor after their defeat; yours with ignominy after conquest.
IGNOMINIOUS, a. Incurring disgrace; cowardly; of mean character.
2. Very shameful; reproachful; dishonorable; infamous.
scriptures: Pro 18:3
When the wicked cometh, then cometh also contempt, and with ignominy reproach.
Isa 53:3
He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
Heb 12:2
Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.
Php 2:8
And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach.
corruption_summary: Disgrace is assumed to be a sign of God's displeasure, and the cross is the standing refutation.
corruption_paragraphs: Crucifixion was designed to be shameful. Rome had faster ways to kill and chose this one because it stripped, exposed and displayed a man at a crossroads for as long as possible, reserved for slaves and rebels; Cicero said the very word should be kept far from the ears of Roman citizens. Philippians 2:8 tracks the descent deliberately — He humbled Himself, became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross — with that last clause added as the floor beneath the floor. The most disgraced man in Jerusalem that day was the only innocent one, which permanently severs the link between shame and guilt.

Hebrews 12:2 says He endured the cross despising the shame, and the verb is worth pausing on. He did not fail to feel it; He counted it as of no weight against the joy set before Him. That is not stoicism but a valuation — He measured the disgrace against what it purchased and found it light. This is the exact pattern the chapter recommends to believers under discipline and reproach, and it depends entirely on there being something on the other side of the scale.

Hebrews 13:13 turns it into a summons and it is not comfortable. Let us go forth unto Him without the camp, bearing His reproach — outside the place of respectability, where the bodies of the sin offerings were burned. A Christianity arranged so that its adherents never lose standing has not understood the geography. The verse's consolation is in the next line: for here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come. The name a man loses out there is not the name he is finally known by.
roots_summary: Hebrew qalon (H7036), shame, ignominy; cherpah (H2781), reproach; Greek aischune (G152), shame; oneidismos (G3680), reproach.
roots_lines: Hebrew qalon (H7036) — shame, ignominy; Proverbs 18:3, 11:2, 13:18, Jeremiah 13:26.
Greek kataphroneo aischunes (G2706, G152) — despising the shame; Hebrews 12:2.
Greek oneidismos (G3680) — reproach; Hebrews 13:13, 11:26, 10:33, Romans 15:3.
usage: “With ignominy reproach” — the AV's one use of the word.
“Even the death of the cross” — the floor beneath the floor.
“Without the camp, bearing his reproach” — and it is a summons.
